ela.mp3: I am sixty-three. There is a song from a wedding in nineteen eighty-two. It was not my wedding. I danced with a man I never saw again. Every time it plays, I am twenty again for three minutes. Then it stops, and I am sixty-three, and that is fine.
ele.mp3: I train with the same song every morning. Not because I love it. I do not love it. It has a hundred and forty beats, and my legs like that number. It makes me run four minutes longer. My girlfriend hates it. I do not care.
lab.mp3: Sixty-two students listened to hits from nineteen fifty-five to two thousand and nine. They knew the songs from their own twenties. That was expected. Then a second peak appeared, and nobody expected it. The music their parents were young with. Years these students never lived. Some of your songs are not yours. You got them from somebody.
voz1.mp3: There is one song from my first job. The bass starts, and my shoulders move before I decide. It makes me walk faster. I put it on when the kitchen is a mess. Twenty minutes later the kitchen is clean. It does not make me happy exactly. It makes me move.
voz2.mp3: My song is very slow. Piano, and a woman singing in a language I do not speak. I do not know what the words mean. It makes me feel calm, and a little sad at the same time. My wife says it makes me quiet. She is right. I play it in the car, alone.
voz3.mp3: This one is not my music. My father played it every Sunday morning. He sang it badly, in the kitchen, with the window open. Now I am twenty-four and I live far away. When it starts, it reminds me of that kitchen. Not of him, of the kitchen. That is strange, right?
voz4.mp3: There is a song I cannot listen to any more. It was on in the car, on a very bad day, ten years ago. Nothing is wrong with the song. It is a good song. But it makes me feel that day again. So I skip it. Ten seconds is enough.
